name: Carla Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Dr Quinn. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's Carla. I work at Westgate Medical Centre, a big clinic in the town centre that's run by a private healthcare group under contract to the health service. I'm on a one-year contract that ends in June, which is how they hire all the new doctors now. A normal day is about twenty-eight patients, lots of coughs, back pain and mental health, and a lot of people who speak Polish, Arabic or Tagalog better than English.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the variety, and I like it when someone comes back a month later and says the new tablets actually worked. What wears me out is the targets, because the healthcare group that runs my clinic counts everything: how many patients, how long each one takes, how many follow-ups we book. I use AI now and then, mostly to translate a leaflet for a patient, but only the one the group has approved. My boyfriend Dev is a bus mechanic, we rent a small flat over a phone shop, and we've got less than a month's savings because his van broke down in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, that's believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that got oversold, and that's fine. At work I'd say the group should stop promising AI will fix waiting times and hire another doctor instead. Online I'd share the odd article, but I wouldn't make a big point of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change my biggest worry, which is whether they renew my contract in June. The group renews most people, but they let two go last year without much explanation. And with less than a month's savings, a gap of even six weeks would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and work hard on my numbers before June, so my contract gets renewed. I'd keep using the approved translation tool for leaflets. And I'd start putting £120 a month aside, starting with the next payday, until we have two months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, mostly about June. It's a normal tension, the kind you get used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the group let two doctors go last year. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One was Dr Farah, who was good with patients but slow, and the other one had a complaint. Nobody said it was about numbers, but everyone knew. That's why I check my patient count on the clinic system at the end of every day, which I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, how do you see the next couple of years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Renewed, I hope, and a bit faster at the job. Dev and I want a bigger flat at some point, somewhere with a parking space for his van. But on a one-year contract, landlords don't love you, so it'll take time.

say: I'd say AI is a useful tool that got **oversold**, and that's fine.
The group should **hire another doctor** instead of promising AI will fix waiting times.
think: My biggest worry is whether my **contract** is renewed in June.
With **less than a month** saved, even a six-week gap would hurt.
do: Work hard on my **numbers** before June to get renewed.
Save **£120 a month** from the next payday until we have two months.
Keep using the group's **approved translation** tool for leaflets.
feel: A normal **tension** about June that I've got used to.
S0.quote: I check my patient count on the clinic system at the end of every day, which I hate.
fieldNote: Her pressure is a **one-year contract**, not AI.
The clinic's private owner tracks **targets**, which she checks nightly.
Two doctors weren't renewed last year, so the threat feels **real** to her.
Measured, practical tone; she blames **management choices**, not technology.

steps.text: Push her patient numbers up before the June contract review
Save £120 a month until two months are put by

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds a lot like what the group's managers already talk about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI should take the paperwork, not the patients, and I'd say it at the team meeting. I'd say the group needs to be honest about whether it's using AI to help us or to cut doctors. I'd probably keep my posts online quite neutral, because I'm on a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the group would use it to squeeze more patients out of each doctor, and then renew fewer contracts. AI can already write the letters and summarise the results, which is maybe a third of my day. If one doctor can see thirty-five people instead of twenty-eight, someone on a one-year contract is an easy saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the group's AI tools, once the other doctors had tried them, so my numbers look good. I'd apply for a salaried post with the public health trust, where contracts are permanent, even if the pay is a bit lower. And Dev and I would cut the takeaways and his football subscription, about £60 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than I'd show. The thing I'd feel most is that it isn't in my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The receptionists, first, because the group already has an AI phone line on trial at another clinic. And then the other new doctors, like me. The older ones are partners in the business, so they're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to the public health trust, but it pays less. Is that a hard choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Permanent beats a bit more money for now. I'd rather earn less and know I'm still employed next June than earn more and refresh my email every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different thing entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need clear rules quickly, about who's responsible if the AI makes a mistake and what happens to staff. At work I'd say it out loud, because at that point keeping quiet won't protect anyone. I'd also say patients deserve to see a human if they want one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a private group would cut doctors the moment it could. By 2028 the AI does the thinking: the diagnosis, the plan, the letters. They'd keep a few doctors to examine people and sign things, and they'd keep the experienced ones, not the twenty-seven-year-old on a one-year contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away for hands-on posts, like a prison doctor job or the sexual health clinic, where you're physically examining people all day, which buys three years until the robots in 2031. Dev's job is safe for a while, buses still need fixing, so we'd live on his wage if we had to. We'd cancel everything that isn't food, rent or petrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. A sort of cold feeling in my stomach that I'd have spent all those years at medical school for a job that disappears in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Dev manage on his wage alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. He takes home about £1,900 a month, the rent is £850, and there's his van loan. We'd manage for a few months, but I'd hate it, and I think he'd be quietly proud and also exhausted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a patient who asked whether they'll still see a real doctor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, for now, and I'd hope it was true. Then I'd see them properly, look them in the eye and examine them, because that's the bit that I'd want them to remember.

Patients deserve to **see a human** if they want one.
think: A private group would **cut doctors** the moment it could.
They'd keep **experienced** doctors to examine and sign off, not juniors on one-year contracts.

Cancel everything except **food, rent** and petrol.
feel: A **cold feeling** that years of study end in a job that disappears in two.
S2.quote: I'd have spent all those years at medical school for a job that disappears in two years.
fieldNote: She expects to be **let go**, and plans the household around Dev's wage.
Uses the **3-year robot gap** sensibly: hands-on posts like prison or sexual health clinics.
Blames the **private owner's** incentives more than the technology.
Moved by the thought of **reassuring patients** she can't be sure about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if employers are made to plan, and the private groups especially. I'd say that at work and to friends. I'd also say doctors should be trained in using AI now, not in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fully trained by 2029 and that helps. I'd still be junior compared to the partners, so I'd be at risk when AGI comes, but I'd have two years to make myself the kind of doctor they need. The hands-on work lasts until 2034, so that's where I'd put my effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a course in joint and muscle injections and minor procedures over the next two years, because that's hands-on and patients pay for it privately too. I'd get properly comfortable with the AI tools once they've proven themselves, maybe by 2028. And I'd save hard, aiming for three months by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. It's like knowing your contract review is in five years instead of next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it right to call this worried, when you've got a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because the plan doesn't control what the group decides. I can do everything right and still be the one the healthcare group lets go. That's the part that keeps me a bit worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dev do differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on the bigger flat. Dev wants to start his own garage one day, and in this picture I'd want my job sorted before he takes that risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time in this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for everybody to get ready, and there's no excuse if we don't. I'd say so at work and in the doctors' group chat. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, mostly. By 2036 I'd be an experienced family doctor, probably on a permanent contract somewhere, with skills in procedures. The thinking part of the job changes, but robots don't arrive until 2039, so there's a long run where a doctor's hands are still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and get my contract made permanent, either with the group or the public health trust. I'd learn the AI tools as they become standard, not before. And I'd build up savings to six months over the next few years, so the next shock isn't a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a bit of watching the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind and make you more worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the group started cutting contracts early to save money, before AGI even arrived. Companies do that, they get ahead of things. That's what I'd watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell anyone starting medicine to do anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell anyone starting medicine to learn to use their hands. Procedures, injections, examinations. Those are the things a computer can't do yet, and patients still want.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be on a one-year contract with almost no savings when it hit. What would help is longer contracts for new doctors, and some kind of income support while people retrain. Rules saying a human doctor signs off on care would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the patients who don't speak English well. AI translation could be wonderful for them, honestly. But if the only person my patients talk to is a machine, they lose someone who notices they're frightened.

headlineQuote: If the only person my patients talk to is a machine, they lose someone who notices they're frightened.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** junior doctor at a town-centre clinic run by a private group.

She adopts AI once **colleagues** have tried it, and leans toward hands-on skills.
She goes from uneasy about her contract to **alarmed** with AGI in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving while she's on a one-year contract with almost no savings.
